based_on: The owner's approved text for each design, read from the database (Signature Cap's design story and imagery meaning on 2026-10-16, the rest on 2026-10-15).
note: Suggested wording only, rewritten with the awebound-brand voice (Sound like a person). The owner's content editor offers it; nothing is saved until the owner saves, approves or publishes. Server-only: never import into client code.

behold:thorns-to-lilies.biblicalContext:
Isaiah 1 is addressed to Judah and Jerusalem. The temple was busy. People brought their sacrifices, kept the festivals and prayed long prayers, while the poor were cheated and widows and orphans had no one to speak for them. God tells them He is tired of their offerings and won’t listen to their prayers, because their hands are full of blood.

Then, in verse 18, He invites them to come and settle the matter with Him. Their sins are as red as scarlet and crimson, and He promises to make them as white as snow and wool. The God who has just named everything they’ve done wrong is the same God offering to wash it away.

The verses around it show what coming back looks like. He tells them to stop doing wrong and learn to do right, to seek justice, defend the oppressed and take up the cause of orphans and widows. The passage is honest about the other road too. Those who refuse and keep rebelling will face judgment.
behold:thorns-to-lilies.designStory:
Thorns to Lilies puts the weight of sin and the hope of being made clean into one image. A crown of thorns circles the wordmark, and partway around, the thorns break open into lilies. The crown points to Christ’s suffering. The lilies stand for the new life that grows out of it.

The design comes from Isaiah 1:18, where God invites His people back to Him and promises to wash out a stain as deep as scarlet. Coming back starts with being honest about sin and receiving His forgiveness. It shows up afterward in everyday choices and in how other people are treated, and the lilies are a picture of a life God is still restoring.

behold:to-live-is-christ.biblicalContext:
Paul wrote Philippians from prison. He didn’t know whether he would be released or executed, and following Jesus had already cost him his freedom. What mattered most to him was that Christ would be honored either way.

He weighs the two outcomes plainly. If he lives, he can keep working, strengthening the church and helping the believers in Philippi grow in their faith. If he dies, he will be with Christ, which he calls better by far. Being sure of that future doesn’t make him careless about the present. He expects to stay, because they still need him.

Later in the same letter, Paul looks back at everything he once counted as an achievement and calls it loss next to the worth of knowing Christ Jesus. He says he has lost all of it for Christ’s sake and counts it as garbage, so that he can gain Christ.
behold:to-live-is-christ.designStory:
To Live Is Christ, To Die Is Gain sets an hourglass inside Paul’s words. Sand running through the glass makes time something you can see, and it raises a plain question about where the days are going.

Above the sand there’s a cross, and below it a seed has started to sprout. Paul’s sentence wraps around both. Ordinary days can be given to Christ while there’s time to give them, and the seed points to a life with Him that keeps going after the last grain falls.

behold:by-his-hem.biblicalContext:
Matthew 9 tells of a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years. Mark’s account adds that she had suffered under many doctors and spent everything she had, and she only got worse. By the time she came near Jesus, she had nothing left to try.

She came up behind Him in the crowd and touched the edge of His cloak, telling herself that if she could only touch it, she would be healed. Jesus turned, saw her and called her daughter. He told her that her faith had healed her.

The crowd was pressing in on every side, and Jesus still stopped for her. Mark records that He told her to go in peace, freed from her suffering.
behold:by-his-hem.designStory:
By His Hem keeps its focus on a hand and the edge of a cloak. It’s a small gesture, and behind it are twelve years of need and the nerve to reach for Jesus with whatever strength was left.

A hand held out like that has nothing to offer and nothing to explain. It just reaches. The folds of the cloak and the spray of rust pull the eye into the moment she touches it, where her suffering meets His compassion.

She came to Jesus as she was, need and all, and He turned to her.

behold:stone-in-motion.biblicalContext:
Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to look at Jesus’ tomb. There was a violent earthquake, and an angel rolled the stone back and sat on it. He told the women not to be afraid. Jesus wasn’t there. He had risen, just as He said, and they could come and see the place where He had lain.

They hurried off to tell the disciples, afraid and full of joy at the same time, and on the way Jesus Himself met them. They took hold of His feet and worshiped Him. He told them not to be afraid and to tell His brothers to go to Galilee, where they would see Him.

Paul later writes in 1 Corinthians 15 that everything rests on this. If Christ hasn’t been raised, faith is futile. Because He has, He is the first of many, and those who belong to Him will be raised too.
behold:stone-in-motion.designStory:
Stone in Motion starts at the tomb, a place that was supposed to be the end. The stone has rolled aside, and the sweep of blue around it keeps it moving, carrying the eye to the angel’s words at the center of the piece.

The moved stone is a witness to an empty grave. The blue gives the artwork its energy, and the words explain why the stone is moving at all.

It puts the news of the empty tomb on an everyday shirt. The One who was crucified is alive.

behold:still-the-storm.biblicalContext:
In Mark 4, it’s evening, and Jesus tells the disciples to cross to the other side of the lake. They set out at His word. Partway across, a furious squall hits. Waves break over the boat and it starts to fill with water, while Jesus sleeps in the stern on a cushion. They wake Him and ask if He cares that they’re about to drown.

He gets up, rebukes the wind and tells the waves to be still, and everything goes completely calm. Then He asks why they’re so afraid and whether they still have no faith. Their fear turns into awe, and they ask each other who this is, that even the wind and the waves obey Him.

Psalm 107 describes sailors caught in a storm who cry out to the Lord, and He stills the storm to a whisper. The disciples had just watched Jesus do what that psalm says God does.
behold:still-the-storm.designStory:
Still the Storm is built around the force of the water. On the front, storm waves break through the Awebound wordmark. On the back, a wave rises under the disciples’ question, the kind of sea no one in that boat could control.

Mark ends the story with their question still hanging in the air, and the design leaves it there too. Who is this, that even the wind and the waves obey Him?

The design comes from reverence for Christ, whose voice the storm obeyed. Fear and the need to stay in control can be brought to Him.
behold:still-the-storm.imageryMeaning: The breaking wave gives visible form to the danger and force of the storm. On the front, the same storm breaks through the Awebound wordmark. Its printed King James wording remains intact while website quotations use NIV.

behold:torn-veil.biblicalContext:
Matthew records that the moment Jesus died, the curtain in the temple tore in two from top to bottom. The earth shook, rocks split, and the centurion guarding Him said that surely He was the Son of God. That curtain closed off the Most Holy Place. Hebrews 9 explains that only the high priest could go behind it, once a year, and never without blood.

Hebrews 10 says believers can now enter God’s presence with confidence, by the blood of Jesus, through a new and living way He opened for them through the curtain, His own body. With Him as their great priest, they’re told to draw near with a sincere heart and the full assurance that faith brings.

The letter goes on to urge them to hold on to their hope without wavering and to spur one another on toward love and good deeds.
behold:torn-veil.designStory:
Torn Veil shows the temple curtain ripped open, with light pouring through above the clouds. The tear gives the piece its movement. The light stands for the hope on the other side, the way to God that Christ opened.

Every fold and gap in the red fabric points to what His death made possible, and the opening reads as an invitation to come near.

The design holds reverence and gratitude together, because the way in cost Jesus His life. What it means carries on past the artwork, into prayer and worship and a life that answers His grace.

behold:the-passage.biblicalContext:
Psalm 23 pictures the Lord as a shepherd who provides for His sheep, gives them rest and leads them along the right paths. The psalm moves from green pastures and quiet waters into the darkest valley, and the Shepherd’s care goes the whole way.

In the valley, David’s words change. Until then he has been talking about the Lord. Now he speaks to Him directly, saying he won’t fear any evil because the Lord is with him. The rod and staff that guide and guard the sheep are what comfort him. Even the table God prepares for him is set in front of his enemies.

The psalm never pretends the valley isn’t there. It holds the danger inside a larger confidence in God’s care. Jesus later called Himself the good shepherd, who knows His sheep and lays down His life for them.
behold:the-passage.designStory:
Fear Not carries David’s words from Psalm 23:4, “I will fear no evil,” in tall letters of cracked stone. Each letter holds a mountain valley with pines and a winding path, and red cracks run through the last word.

The name comes from those words. There’s a road to walk and a dark stretch to get through, and the Shepherd is near for all of it. God is with the one who walks.

The piece is a quiet confession of dependence on Him. When the way ahead isn’t clear, the words point back to His presence and the next faithful step.
behold:the-passage.imageryMeaning: The dark valley, the pines and the winding path inside the stone letters give the psalm a journey to follow. The red cracks run through “evil,” the word David says he won’t fear. The words keep God’s presence at the heart of the scene.
behold:the-passage.shareCopy: The Shepherd is present in the valley. Fear Not is inspired by Psalm 23:4.

behold:wonderfully-made.biblicalContext:
Psalm 139 is a prayer full of wonder at how completely God knows the one praying. He knows when David sits down and when he gets up, what he’s thinking from far away and what he’ll say before he says it. In verses 13 to 16, David turns to his own beginning. God formed him in his mother’s womb and saw him before he was born.

Being fearfully and wonderfully made sends David into praise. His attention stays on the Creator, who wrote down every one of his days before any of them happened. Genesis 1 says people are made in God’s image, and read together, the two passages give a reason to treat every human life with dignity and care.

The psalm ends with David asking God to search his heart, to see if there’s any offensive way in him, and to lead him in the way everlasting.
behold:wonderfully-made.designStory:
Wonderfully Made wraps its lettering in roses and red leaves, so the words look tended, as if someone took their time with them. The flowers bring the beauty, and the Scripture turns it toward the Creator.

A wooden cross stands among the roses and ties the piece to Behold’s focus on Jesus. Between them, there’s room to stop and think about being formed and known by God.

That changes how a person sees themselves, and how they see everyone else. Gratitude for His work leads to gentleness and care toward the people around them.

behold:lambs-mark.biblicalContext:
In John 1, John the Baptist keeps pointing away from himself. He calls himself a voice in the wilderness, sent to prepare the way. When he sees Jesus coming toward him, he tells the people to look, because here is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. They’re asked to think about who Jesus is and what He came to do.

The title points to sacrifice. Isaiah 53 describes a servant led like a lamb to the slaughter, who carries the sins of many. Christians see that costly work fulfilled in Christ.

John also says he saw the Spirit come down from heaven like a dove and stay on Jesus, and he testifies that this is God’s Chosen One.
behold:lambs-mark.designStory:
Lamb’s Mark brings a lamb and a crown of thorns together in one small emblem. The lamb comes from John calling Jesus the Lamb of God. The thorns tie that name to His suffering.

It’s a small image with a lot in it. The gentleness of the lamb sits right next to what the crown cost.

In Behold, this is the simplest way the release asks people to look at Jesus. The mark is easy to notice, and the hope is that it starts conversations that move from the stitching to His sacrifice and the forgiveness found in Him.

behold:signature-cap.biblicalContext:
Ephesians 1 opens with Paul praising God for every spiritual blessing His people have in Christ. In the middle of that praise, he says they have redemption through Jesus’ blood and the forgiveness of sins, given out of the riches of God’s grace. Those gifts belong to a bigger story of being adopted into God’s family, and of His plan to bring everything in heaven and on earth together under Christ.

Redemption means being bought back at a cost. Paul grounds it in what Jesus did, and he turns the thanks toward the grace God gave freely.

Ephesians 2 shows what that grace produces. Salvation comes by grace through faith, as God’s gift, and the people He makes alive in Christ are created to do the good works He prepared for them in advance.
behold:signature-cap.designStory:
The Signature Cap is Awebound’s name in its own lettering, with red thorns reaching out from both sides. Crimson runs through the ivory letters, so the meaning of the thorns carries right into the name.

The thorns recall the crown Christ wore. The red is for the blood He shed to redeem us, and it keeps the name rooted in His sacrifice.

The tagline says why the cap exists. Bound in awe is reverence for Jesus. Worn without shame is being willing to be known as His. The cap goes wherever the person wearing it goes, as a reminder to reflect Him in how they speak and how they treat people.
behold:signature-cap.imageryMeaning: The red thorn branches recall the crown Christ wore, and the crimson running through the ivory letters is a reminder of His sacrifice. They tie Awebound’s name to what Behold is about, looking to Jesus and the redemption found in Him.
